prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the time-reversal-invariant quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Reading the mandate literally, B018 is a discovery with a verifiable chain: Kane and Mele predicted a new topological class of insulator with protected edge conduction, and Molenkamp's group then saw the quantised edge transport in HgTe quantum wells in 2007, which is the original experiment. The result has been reproduced for almost two decades in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and, through ARPES and transport, the three-dimensional Bi-based compounds, so there is no maturity concern and I am confident that nature confirmed the picture. It opened a door to phenomena nobody could previously see, and it changed how electronic matter is classified. Of the shortlisted candidates it is the one where I am closest to being 'absolutely sure' about both the topic and the verified result. Its six-member opening support, with five top-three placements, also reflects scientific breadth across condensed matter, materials and device physics, though I do not treat support as merit.
statement.case_against: The credit is genuinely incomplete. The HgTe experiment was guided by the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and Shoucheng Zhang is deceased and cannot be honoured, while Fu-Kane and Moore-Balents on 3D topological insulators and the first ARPES observations (Hasan and others) sit outside both the credited names and the three-laureate limit. If the historical record shows BHZ was the decisive step for the experiment, then Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would honour the 2005 concept and a 2007 experiment that followed a different proposal. I also recall this history from memory, and the committee should check it against the primary papers. A second reservation is that practical benefit is still prospective, so the case rests on understanding of nature rather than on technology.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B018 first as a clean, verified theory-to-experiment discovery, overdue rather than premature, but flags that BHZ and the 3D ARPES work are not covered, and wonders about pairing with the quantum anomalous Hall effect or treating B004 as a competing framing.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and on the theory-to-experiment arc. Where I would go further is on the attribution: the 2D quantum spin Hall experiment is the original verification, and I would keep the citation tied to that and to the Z2 prediction rather than widen it to quantum anomalous Hall, which is a later and separate experimental discovery (and B004 is not on the shortlist). Widening the citation to the 3D story would invite exactly the credit disputes we cannot resolve with three names. I would rather state the omission openly in the committee record.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics (B032) first for exact, model-independent relations, and ranks B018 second with the gap in credit for BHZ and the 3D work.
responses.response: I take the elegance and universality of B032 seriously, and as a statistical-physics argument it is hard to fault. My concern is the one the committee has to apply to every candidate: the original experiments. The theorems were tested later in tweezer, colloid and single-electron experiments, and priority among Evans, Gallavotti-Cohen, Jarzynski, Crooks, Kurchan and Seifert is, by your own account, unsettled, with some of them outside our credited names. B018 has a sharper original experiment and a cleaner trio. I would keep B032 as a serious later candidate but I do not see it resolving the attribution problem soon.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B020) first as a clean platform discovery, ranks B018 third, and notes that credit for BHZ and the 3D case is spread across more people than three, while flagging his own ties to WACQT.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour on the conflict, and I think it is right that you weigh it and defer on B020. On B018 we agree about the attribution gap. Where I differ is on B020: the four-name credit has a genuine theory-versus-experiment allocation problem (Blais versus Girvin), and the 2025 prize for superconducting circuits, as Kroll also recalls, sits close in time. That is a larger structural obstacle than the BHZ omission, which concerns who is added rather than which of several equal claimants is dropped.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock (B041) first as an experimentally concrete new measurement method with 10^-18 uncertainty, and asks whether it is sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes.
responses.response: I share the enthusiasm, as B041 is my third choice and a tool that opens a door. The overlap question is precisely my reservation: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium demonstration are original, but Ye's contribution is arguably a later, better-performing realisation, and I would not want the citation to read as a lifetime or performance prize. If the committee wants B041 I would draft the citation around the magic-wavelength lattice concept and make the distinction from 2005 and 2012 explicit. I do not think the case is stronger than B018, but it is a credible alternative.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B041 first and B018 fourth, valuing the topological state as a new phase distinguished by topology rather than symmetry breaking, while noting that credit is incomplete (Zhang, Bernevig, Fu, Hasan).
responses.response: Your framing of B018 as a new phase of matter fits my own view of it. On the clock, I agree it is clear and timely, but I am less comfortable that two names are the whole story, since parallel contributions (for example Lemonde and Gill, as you mention) and the comb and ion-clock lineage already recognised complicate it. I would not oppose a prize for B041 but I would rank it behind B018 because the original experiment and the people are clearer for the topological insulators.

uncertainties: Whether BHZ and 3D topological insulator contributors (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Hasan) were decisive enough that the credit for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would be judged incomplete.
Whether the committee should word the citation around the 2D quantum spin Hall effect only, or include the 3D topological insulators, given the three-person limit.
My recollection of dates and priority is from memory and has not been checked against the primary literature.
For B041, how much of the credit belongs to Katori's original magic-wavelength proposal versus later performance work by Ye.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B018, B041 or B030. I note that Göran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague and has flagged his own ties to the circuit-QED community (B020), which is not in my preferred configuration. I have no known collaboration with the credited candidates.
